entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Anton Graff (1736–1813) was a Swiss-born portrait painter who became the pre-eminent likeness-maker of German-speaking Enlightenment and early Romantic elites, long based in Dresden. His sitters included rulers, officers, scholars, and poets—faces of the late Holy Roman Empire’s cultured public rendered with sober psychological presence rather than Baroque pomp.

Graff’s Dresden career placed him at a crossroads of Saxon court patronage and a widening bourgeois market for portraits. He helped define how the German Enlightenment wished to see itself: intelligent, restrained, and individually characterised. Many canonical images of writers and statesmen survive through his brush.

Art historians rank him among the great eighteenth-century European portraitists, a northern counterpart to Reynolds or Duplessis in creating an age’s visual archive of persons.
